messages.author: c858c4512669f1a1
messages.subject: Interpreting population level RSF outputs
parts:
Hi Chris,

I'm using the rsf.select() function to estimate population-level resource selection of certain covariates over a large study area. I have a lot of individuals with small(ish) home range sizes so they arent all exposed to the same types of landscapes. Because of this, we have decided to do a model selection to see what covariates drive selection for each individual. If the individual has a covariate listed in its top model, we obtain an estimate for that individual and that particular covariate. However, we have a handful of individuals that don't have some of the covariates in their top models thus we have some "NAs" as placeholders for these.  

Could you explain what happens under the hood when the mean() function is applied to the rsf.select output? Lets say, for example, I have a list of beta values for a particular covariate (0.23, 0.45, 0.54, NA, NA, 0.11). What would occur in this case?

Because I have many individuals without estimates for some of the parameters, I want to make sure I know whats going on and how the population mean is being calculated to determine if this makes sense or not. I looked at the averages and they don't seem to particularly match up with the mean output so it makes me wonder if some sort of weighting is occurring? 

Thank you so much and I apologize if I missed this in an already existing thread.

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Interpreting population level RSF outputs
parts:
Hi Mikiah,

In the meta-analytic regression, the missing estimates are assigned infinite uncertainty (zero weight).

In the univariate case, the weight of each estimate is 1/(uncertainty + population variance), where the population variance is simultaneously estimated.
In the multivariate case, correlations also inform the weights.

mean() is using a normal-normal meta-analysis (hierarchical model) after a log transform of the scale parameters and log(chi^2) bias correction.

Best,
Chris
